content: In studies conducted among high-risk groups in various settings, circumcised men demonstrated a 71% reduction in the risk of HIV infection compared to uncircumcised men. However, the protective effect was less consistent than in studies involving the general male population. These studies included sexually transmitted infection (STI) clinic patients in Nairobi, Kenya; trucking company employees in Mombasa, Kenya; STI clinic patients in India; men in Uganda with HIV-positive wives during a time when HIV status awareness was low; and HIV-negative men in stable serodiscordant relationships with HIV-positive female partners before widespread antiretroviral therapy (ART) coverage. Community-based studies conducted before the scale-up of voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC) showed an overall 52% reduction in HIV risk among circumcised men compared to uncircumcised men. This reduced risk was observed in regions where male circumcision was both less common (e.g., Uganda and India) and more common (e.g., Kenya). In six communities where VMMC prevalence and ART coverage were simultaneously increasing due to programmatic efforts (e.g., Kenya, South Africa, and Uganda), the reduction in HIV incidence among circumcised men compared to uncircumcised men was 44%, with consistent findings across studies. Combined results from all observational studies indicated a 50% lower HIV risk among circumcised men. The absolute reduction in HIV infection risk was estimated at 13 fewer infections per 1,000 person-years in post-randomized controlled trial (RCT) follow-up studies over six years, 9 fewer infections per 1,000 person-years in community-based studies before VMMC scale-up, and 7 fewer infections per 1,000 person-years during the VMMC scale-up. Among high-risk cohorts, the absolute reduction was 39 fewer infections per 1,000 person-years, highlighting the greater impact of male circumcision in settings with high HIV incidence. The evidence supporting the direct effect of VMMC on reducing HIV risk among heterosexual men is of high quality. In communities with increasing VMMC and ART coverage, HIV prevalence was 35% lower among circumcised men compared to uncircumcised men. For example, in Rakai, Uganda, between 1999 and 2013, each 10% increase in circumcision prevalence was associated with a 13% reduction in male HIV incidence. Similarly, each 10% increase in ART coverage among women was linked to a 5% reduction in male HIV incidence. HIV-negative women may also benefit directly from a reduced risk of transmission if their HIV-positive male partners are circumcised. However, an RCT found an increased risk of HIV transmission to female partners in the first six months after circumcision if the male partner was not on ART and resumed sexual activity before the circumcision wound had fully healed. This underscores the importance of ensuring that HIV-positive men are on ART and virally suppressed before undergoing circumcision. VMMC has already prevented a significant number of HIV infections. Modeling estimates suggest that nearly 23 million circumcisions performed by the end of 2018 in 15 priority countries in East and Southern Africa averted approximately 250,000 new HIV infections. By 2030, this number is projected to reach 5 million, given the lifelong partial protection offered by VMMC. Even with the scale-up of other prevention interventions, such as ART, VMMC remains a critical component of HIV prevention strategies. In addition to its HIV prevention benefits, VMMC has been associated with reductions in other sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and conditions such as bacterial vaginosis and cervical cancer. For instance, modeling in Uganda suggests that VMMC scale-up alone could prevent about 20% of cervical cancer cases in scenarios with limited HPV vaccination and cervical cancer screening. VMMC programs also provide opportunities to deliver additional health services, such as HIV testing, safer sex education, STI management, and linkage to care for HIV-positive individuals. These programs have integrated services like hypertension screening, tuberculosis screening, and family planning, further enhancing their public health impact. While VMMC is generally safe, adverse events (AEs) such as bleeding, infection, and wound disruption can occur but are typically rare and manageable. The risk of serious AEs, such as tetanus, can be mitigated through proper vaccination and adherence to safety protocols. Monitoring and quality assurance efforts are essential to minimize these risks further. The acceptability of VMMC is high among men and women, with many viewing it as beneficial for HIV prevention, improved hygiene, and potential sexual health benefits. However, barriers such as fear of pain, complications, and time off work remain. Addressing these concerns through targeted messaging, youth-friendly services, and parental engagement can improve uptake, particularly among adolescents. In conclusion, VMMC is a highly effective intervention for reducing HIV incidence and offers additional health benefits.
